paper_title: On the triviality of the unramified Iwasawa modules of the maximal multiple $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extensions

candidates.claim_content:
Setting. Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $M$ be a free $\mathbb{Z}_p$-module of rank $4$ with basis $\gamma, x, y, z$ (written multiplicatively: a general element is $\gamma^{g}x^{\alpha}y^{\beta}z^{\delta}$ with $g,\alpha,\beta,\delta\in\mathbb{Z}_p$). Fix $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}_p$. Let $J$ be the $\mathbb{Z}_p$-module automorphism of $M$ determined by
$$J(x)=x^{-1},\quad J(y)=y^{-1},\quad J(z)=z^{-1},\quad J(\gamma)=\gamma x^{a-b-c}y^{a+b-c}z^{a+b+c}.$$
(In the paper, $M=\mathrm{Gal}(\widetilde{k}/k)\simeq\mathbb{Z}_p^{\oplus 4}$ for a CM-field $k$ of degree $6$ in which the odd prime $p$ splits completely and which satisfies Leopoldt's conjecture; $\widetilde{k}$ is the maximal multiple $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of $k$; $\gamma$ is a topological generator of the inertia group $I_1$ of a prime $\mathfrak{p}_1\mid p$; $x,y,z\in X(k_{\mathrm{cyc}})=\mathrm{Gal}(\widetilde{k}/k_{\mathrm{cyc}})$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(\widetilde{k}/k)=\langle\gamma,x,y,z\rangle$ and $X(k_{\mathrm{cyc}})=\langle x,y,z\rangle$; $J$ is the complex conjugation, which acts as $-1$ on $X(k_{\mathrm{cyc}})$, and $J(\gamma)=\gamma x^{a-b-c}y^{a+b-c}z^{a+b+c}$ is the stated generator of the inertia group $\overline{I}_1$ in Lemma 4.1.4.)

Standing hypotheses of Section 4.3: $a+b\equiv 0 \pmod p$ with $m:=\mathrm{ord}_p(a+b)$ satisfying $0<m<\infty$ (so $a+b\neq 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_p$), $a-c\not\equiv 0 \pmod p$ and $b+c\not\equiv 0 \pmod p$.

Claim to check. The two closed $\mathbb{Z}_p$-submodules
$$H_1:=\langle \gamma x^{a-c},\, xy^{-1}z,\, xy\rangle, \qquad H_2:=\langle J(\gamma)\gamma,\, xy^{-1}z,\, xy\rangle$$
of $M$ are equal, and consequently $H_1$ is stable under $J$ and $J$ acts as $-1$ on the rank-one quotient $M/H_1$.

Since $a+b
eq 0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and $p$ is odd, this fails: $J(\gamma)\gamma
otin H_1$. Reducing $J(\gamma)\gamma$ modulo $\langle xy^{-1}z, xyangle$ gives $H_2=\langle \gamma x^{-(a+2b+c)}, xy^{-1}z, xyangle$, and $(a-c)+(a+2b+c)=2(a+b)
eq 0$, so the exponent in the paper is correct only modulo $p^m$, not in $\mathbb{Z}_p$. candidates.error_location: Proof of Corollary 4.1.6, the rank case distinction for $\overline{A'}$
candidates.claim_content:
Let $p$ be a prime, $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}_p$, and let $N$ be a free $\mathbb{Z}_p$-module of rank $4$ with basis $\gamma,x,y,z$. Let $\phi:N\to N$ be the $\mathbb{Z}_p$-linear map with matrix
$$A' := \begin{bmatrix}1&0&0&0\\0&a&b&c\\0&-c&a&b\\0&-b&-c&a\end{bmatrix}$$
with respect to that basis, and let $A(k):=\mathrm{coker}(\phi)$ (this is the paper's presentation of the $p$-Sylow subgroup $A(k)$ of the ideal class group, obtained from $A(k)\simeq\langle\gamma,x,y,z\rangle/\langle\gamma,\;x^ay^bz^c,\;x^{-c}y^az^b,\;x^{-b}y^{-c}z^a\rangle$). Write $\overline{A'}:=A'\bmod p$, a $4\times 4$ matrix over $\mathbb{F}_p$, and let $A:=\begin{bmatrix}a&b&c\\-c&a&b\\-b&-c&a\end{bmatrix}$ be its lower-right $3\times3$ block, $\overline{A}:=A\bmod p$.

Claim to check: that $A(k)=0 \iff \mathrm{rank}\,\overline{A'}=3$, that $A(k)$ is cyclic $\iff \mathrm{rank}\,\overline{A'}=2$, and that $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}A(k)/pA(k)=2 \iff \mathrm{rank}\,\overline{A'}=1$.
candidates.suspected_defect: The three ranks appear to be off by one. Since $\mathrm{coker}(\phi)/p\,\mathrm{coker}(\phi)=\mathbb{F}_p^4/\mathrm{im}(\overline{A'})$, one has $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}A(k)/pA(k)=4-\mathrm{rank}\,\overline{A'}$, so the correct equivalences for the $4\times 4$ matrix $\overline{A'}$ are $\mathrm{rank}=4$, $3$, $2$ respectively. Equivalently, the values $3,2,1$ are the ranks of the $3\times3$ block $\overline{A}$, since $\mathrm{rank}\,\overline{A'}=1+\mathrm{rank}\,\overline{A}$. (The analogous Corollary 3.1.5 uses a $3\times3$ matrix including the $\gamma$ row, where ranks $3,2,1$ are correct; the degree-6 matrix $A'$ is $4\times4$ and the same numbers were reused.) The conclusions (i)(ii)(iii) of Corollary 4.1.6 themselves are unaffected, since they are read off the $3\times 3$ block.

candidates.claim_content:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}_p$ with $c\equiv b-a \pmod p$. Put $|K|:=2(a+b)\big((a+b)^2+3c^2\big)$.

Claim to check: that $|K|\equiv 8(a+b)(a-ab+b^2) \pmod p$, and that $a^2+bc \equiv b^2-ac \equiv c^2+ab \equiv a-ab+b^2 \pmod p$.
candidates.suspected_defect: The quadratic form appears to be mistyped: the first term should be $a^2$, not $a$. Substituting $c\equiv b-a$ gives $(a+b)^2+3c^2 \equiv (a+b)^2+3(b-a)^2 = 4(a^2-ab+b^2)$, hence $|K|\equiv 8(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2)$; and $a^2+bc\equiv a^2-ab+b^2$, $b^2-ac\equiv a^2-ab+b^2$, $c^2+ab\equiv a^2-ab+b^2$. The paper writes $a-ab+b^2$ (an inhomogeneous expression) in all three places, including the concluding "Hence $a-ab+b^2\not\equiv 0$ by Lemma 4.1.6". The intended quantity $a^2-ab+b^2$ makes the argument correct, so this is a dropped exponent rather than a broken inference.

candidates.exact_quote: Next, we show that \(p\) is unramified in \(k_\infty/k\).
candidates.claim_content:
Setting: $k$ is a CM-field of degree $6$ in which the odd prime $p$ splits completely, satisfying Leopoldt's conjecture, with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}A(k)/pA(k)=2$; $\widetilde{k}$ is the maximal multiple $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of $k$; $P_\infty, Q_\infty$ are the $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extensions of $k$ fixed by $\langle D_1,\overline{D}_1\rangle$ and $\langle D_2,\overline{D}_2\rangle$; $P_\infty Q_\infty/k$ is a $\mathbb{Z}_p^2$-extension; $k_\infty$ is the $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of $k$ inside $P_\infty Q_\infty$ fixed by $\langle Z, xy^{\pm 1+pd}\rangle$. The paragraph's argument establishes: every prime of $k$ above $p$ is ramified in $P_\infty/k$ or in $Q_\infty/k$; $\mathfrak{p}_1,\overline{\mathfrak{p}}_1$ are unramified in $P_\infty Q_\infty/k_\infty$, likewise $\mathfrak{p}_2,\overline{\mathfrak{p}}_2$, and by part (i) also $\mathfrak{p}_3,\overline{\mathfrak{p}}_3$; hence $P_\infty Q_\infty/k_\infty$ is unramified, and the paragraph ends "which implies that $p$ is ramified in $k_\infty/k$".

Claim to check: the paragraph's announced goal, namely that $p$ is UNRAMIFIED in $k_\infty/k$.
candidates.suspected_defect: The announced goal contradicts the paragraph's own conclusion and the use made of it. The argument shows $P_\infty Q_\infty/k_\infty$ is unramified while the primes above $p$ ramify in $P_\infty Q_\infty/k$, which forces the ramification to occur in $k_\infty/k$ — i.e. $p$ IS ramified in $k_\infty/k$, as the last sentence of the paragraph states. Moreover Corollary 2.3.3, which the whole construction serves, requires hypothesis (ii) "any prime ideal in $k$ above $p$ is non-split and ramifies in $k_\infty/k$". So "unramified" in the opening sentence should be "ramified".

candidates.exact_quote: This implies that \(\mathfrak{p}_3\) must be inert in \(P_\infty / k\), and therefore \(\mathfrak{p}_3\) cannot be totally inert in \(P_\infty Q_\infty / P_\infty\). In other words, \(\mathfrak{p}_3\) splits in \(P_\infty Q_\infty / P_\infty\).
candidates.claim_content:
Setting: $k$ is a CM-field of degree $6$, $p$ an odd prime splitting completely in $k$, Leopoldt's conjecture holds for $k$ and $p$, and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}A(k)/pA(k)=2$, so that $a^2+bc\equiv b^2-ac\equiv c^2+ab\equiv 0 \pmod p$ and (Lemma 4.4.2) $a,b,c\not\equiv 0$, $a+b+c\not\equiv 0$, $a+b-c\not\equiv 0 \pmod p$. Inside $\mathrm{Gal}(\widetilde{k}/k)=\langle\gamma,x,y,z\rangle\simeq\mathbb{Z}_p^{\oplus4}$, $P_\infty\leftrightarrow\langle D_1,\overline{D}_1\rangle=\langle\gamma,x,y^{a+b-c}z^{a+b+c}\rangle$ and $Q_\infty\leftrightarrow\langle D_2,\overline{D}_2\rangle$; $k_\infty\subset P_\infty Q_\infty$ is the $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of $k$ constructed in Lemma 4.4.4; $D_i, I_i$ are the decomposition and inertia groups of $\mathfrak{p}_i\mid p$. The paragraph has just established, using $(a^2+bc)+(c^2+ab)\equiv 0$, that
$$\langle D_1,\overline{D}_1,I_3\rangle=\langle\gamma,x,y^{-c}z^a,y^{a+b}z^{b+c}\rangle \;\neq\; \langle D_1,\overline{D}_1,D_3\rangle=\langle\gamma,x,y^{a+b-c},z\rangle=\langle\gamma,x,y,z\rangle,$$
under the assumption (for contradiction) that $\mathfrak{p}_3$ does not split in $P_\infty Q_\infty/k_\infty$, hence not in $P_\infty Q_\infty/k$ nor in $P_\infty Q_\infty/P_\infty$.

Claim to check: that the displayed inequality of subgroups implies $\mathfrak{p}_3$ is inert in $P_\infty/k$, that this in turn implies $\mathfrak{p}_3$ cannot be totally inert in $P_\infty Q_\infty/P_\infty$, and hence that $\mathfrak{p}_3$ splits in $P_\infty Q_\infty/P_\infty$.
candidates.suspected_defect: The chain of inferences is hard to follow and may not be valid as written. The displayed relation says only that the image of $I_3$ in $\mathrm{Gal}(P_\infty/k)\simeq\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a proper (finite-index, hence non-trivial) subgroup while the image of $D_3$ is everything — i.e. $\mathfrak{p}_3$ is non-split and ramified, but not unramified, in $P_\infty/k$, so calling it "inert" is at best a misuse of the word. More seriously, no reason is given for the step "$\mathfrak{p}_3$ inert in $P_\infty/k$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mathfrak{p}_3$ cannot be totally inert in $P_\infty Q_\infty/P_\infty$", and the conclusion "$\mathfrak{p}_3$ splits in $P_\infty Q_\infty/P_\infty$" directly contradicts the sentence that immediately follows it ("since $\mathfrak{p}_3$ does not split in $P_\infty Q_\infty/k$, this is a contradiction"), which is where the contradiction is supposed to come from.
